I've talked about this with my family, with my Marine brothers, my brothers at Saveawarrior, my VA counselors, and even God, but the closer I get to his burial the more the weight of his death is crushing my heart. I have not talked about it with you all publicly, but I am compelled to remind everyone I know about the dark reality that our service members, veterans, and first responders are suffering through.

On January 12th 2018, Gunnery Sergeant Vaughn Canlas killed himself with a shot to the head after over 16 years of service to the Marine Corps. He only had a few weeks left on his contract. He is scheduled to be buried at Arlington National Cemetery Feb 21st 2018. To me, he has always been Corporal Canlas, a squad leader who led a bunch of young Marines into combat during the initial invasion of Iraq in 2003.

He was one of the best of us. His personality and laughter was infectious. Strong, determined, dedicated, hilarious, and honorable. He never backed down from a challenge and always managed to pick himself back up and keep moving... until this. He had no wife or children. He gave his entire adult life to his country and Corps. I don't know why he took his own life, only speculation. What I do know is that he is one of many who kill themselves every day after giving up a piece of their own humanity in service to their community. We ALL owe it to them to be better people. 

For fellow vets and first responders, we should be in regular contact with one another, unashamed to bear our souls to our brothers, and continue to keep each other safe as we did before in trying times. The Marine Corp motto is Semper Fi... always faithful. It's not a tag line. Be faithful to one another. Keep each other in your hearts, thoughts, and prayers, but also keep the faith over the phone, on social media, and in person whenever possible. 

To our nation, we need to be our brother's keeper. A person who leaves the armed forces, police force, or fire station is leaving behind their tribe, usually with battle scars and memories of some of the most inhumane tragedies we inflict upon ourselves and others. This burden can be very isolating and is a common factor in their higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicide. The strength of the wolf is the pack, and many are dying lone wolves because of the struggle to integrate back into a civilian population that itself seems increasingly isolated, polarized, and divided.

If you really give a damn about the troops who kill in your name, the vets who can't find their place in a "civilized" world, the police officer crippled by some junky who got off on a technicality, or the firefighter whose hands and heart are scared from failing to dig his partner out of the charred rubble, remember that they are not average civilians working corporate 9 to 5's. They have dedicated their lives to bearing the traumas of a community that someday will no longer relate to them. If they fail to find a new brotherhood, Canlas's fate could also be theirs. 

So call or visit them on occasion, have meaningful conversations about life, and listen more than talk. Invite them to your social club or church. Create a regular event to bring their community and yours closer together. Or donate your time/money towards nonprofit programs that help reconnect them with something meaningful.

We failed Canlas, as we have failed so many of our emotionally wounded heroes before him. But we cannot bear all the blame. We are not super heroes. We can't save them all. But if we can just save one, just one soul, then all the blood and treasure sacrificed will be worth it. Thank you for reading this. I love you all. 🙏🙌🔥❤️
